reader_situation: Someone reaches for brown sugar in the middle of baking and finds a solid brick in the bag or canister. They want to know whether it has gone bad, how to get it usable right now or by tomorrow, and how to keep the next bag from doing the same thing.
direct_answer: Brown sugar turns hard because the moisture its molasses supplies evaporates. Dried-out sugar is still usable: Domino says brown sugar's shelf life is indefinite and sugar kept in a container in a cool, dry place does not support microbial growth, so hardness is a texture problem. Heat softens it only until it cools; returning moisture is the fix Domino says should leave it soft.
consensus: Brown sugar hardens when it dries out
Store it in an airtight container or tightly closed bag
Soften it with a slice of bread, a damp paper towel, or a terra cotta disk
Microwave it briefly with a damp paper towel for a quick fix
gaps: Heat-based fixes are temporary. Domino says oven-softened (250°F) and microwave-softened brown sugar hardens again as it cools, so measure only what you need right away; Ohio State Extension says the same of its 10-to-20-second microwave method. Only moisture-based methods leave the whole container soft.

Published microwave times run from 10 seconds to 2 minutes because the setups differ: Ohio State gives 10 to 20 seconds with a slice of bread under plastic wrap, WSU Extension 30 seconds under a wet paper towel, UGA says check every 30 seconds under a loosely laid damp towel, and Domino gives 1½ to 2 minutes for about ½ lb under two wet towels plus tightly sealed plastic wrap.

Shelf-life numbers are quality windows, not safety dates: Ohio State's chart says 4 months, UGA and WSU say 4 to 6 months for maximum freshness or flavor, and Domino says best within six months but indefinite shelf life. Ohio State adds that brown sugar will likely still harden after a few months even in an airtight container, so a hard bag is not proof of bad storage.

A no-wait, lasting fix exists: King Arthur, citing pastry chef Stella Parks, adds 3/4 teaspoon (3.5 g) of water per 8 oz of brown sugar in a bag and kneads it until uniform. Combined with King Arthur's 213 g per packed cup, this can be scaled to any amount.

Brown sugar storage is the opposite of white sugar storage. Domino says to keep brown sugar in a cool, moist area and not in the refrigerator, while white granulated sugar hardens from moisture and should be kept airtight; Domino's fix for hardened white sugar is a 150–200°F oven that has been turned off, and UGA's is pounding it in a bag.
Domino says powdered sugar lumps cannot be adequately restored because of its cornstarch, so the brown-sugar fixes don't transfer to it.
Freezing is an option for dry climates or long storage per Domino: thaw 2 to 3 hours and stir gently as it thaws if ice crystals formed.

evidence.claim: Why brown sugar hardens and what softening does
evidence.detail: Brown sugar becomes hard when moisture in the sugar evaporates. Therefore, the various methods used for softening brown sugar are intended to return moisture to the sugar.

evidence.claim: Sugar does not spoil; brown sugar shelf life is indefinite, best within six months
evidence.detail: Sugar stored in a container in a cool, dry location has an indefinite shelf life because it does not support microbial growth. Even though the shelf life of brown sugar is indefinite, it's best to use it within six months of purchase for maximum flavor.

evidence.claim: Domino's quick and microwave softening methods, and that they are temporary
evidence.detail: Quick method: heat hard brown sugar in an oven-safe container at 250 degrees; as soon as it's soft, measure the amount you need right away because it will again harden as it cools; oven-heated sugar is very hot. Microwave: about 1/2 lb of hardened brown sugar in a microwave-safe bowl, covered with two wet (not dripping) white paper towels, bowl tightly covered with plastic wrap, HIGH for 1 1/2 - 2 minutes; divide with fork; microwave-softened sugar hardens as it cools so microwave only the amount you need; microwave ovens vary in power.

Place hardened brown sugar in a tight-sealing container, cover with two dampened (not dripping) paper towels placed over a small piece of plastic wrap or foil on top of the sugar, or use a slice of bread; seal tightly; remove the paper towel or bread after the sugar absorbs the moisture and softens (about two days) and tightly reseal. Sugar should remain soft.

evidence.claim: Storage: cool, moist, not the refrigerator; freezing for dry areas
evidence.detail: Brown sugar should be stored in a cool, moist area in a covered container; or a rustproof container or heavy moisture-proof plastic bag, tightly closed. Don't store brown sugar in the refrigerator. If you are in a very dry area or are going to keep it for a long time, you may want to freeze it. Thaw frozen sugar two or three hours. If ice crystals form after long freezer storage, gently stir the sugar as soon as it thaws to prevent pockets of moisture from causing damage.

evidence.claim: Granulated and powdered sugar behave differently
evidence.detail: Granulated sugar will harden when exposed to any type of moisture; when it gets moist, it develops lumps. Powdered sugar cannot adequately be restored if it forms lumps because of the cornstarch used in the sugar.

evidence.claim: Domino's storage page: alternative moisture sources and the hardened white sugar oven method
evidence.detail: Time-permitting method options: a damp paper-towel-wrapped piece of plastic wrap or foil, a damp terra cotta disk, one or two slices of bread, or one or two large marshmallows in a tightly sealed container; remove after about 2 days or once softened. Granulated sugar can harden in moist or humid conditions; to soften, warm the oven to 150–200°F, turn it off, place the sugar in an oven-safe container for about 15 minutes, tap with a spoon; if it doesn't break apart, leave it in the oven for an hour to dry out. Brown sugar quality is best when consumed within six months of purchase and opening.
evidence.source_title: How to Store Domino Brown Sugar (Domino Sugar)

evidence.claim: Ohio State Extension: brown sugar hardens even airtight; 4-month chart value; microwave with bread
evidence.detail: While airtight containers are suitable for brown sugar storage, it will likely still harden after a few months. To soften brown sugar, place in a bowl with a slice of bread, cover the bowl with plastic wrap and microwave on high for 10 to 20 seconds. The brown sugar will be soft enough to scoop and measure but will harden again once cooled. Chart: brown sugar 4 months, put in airtight container; confectioners' sugar 18 months; granulated sugar 2 years. Granulated sugar, honey, and molasses can last indefinitely.
evidence.source_title: Pantry Food Storage, HYG-5401 (Ohio State University Extension)

evidence.claim: UGA: 4 to 6 months maximum freshness; 250°F oven or microwave checking every 30 seconds; pound hardened white sugar
evidence.detail: Brown sugar keeps maximum freshness for four to six months. Store it in an airtight container to retain moisture and prevent hardening; keep it in its original plastic bag, tightly closed, or transfer to an airtight container or a moisture-proof plastic bag. To soften, heat in a 250-degree oven for a few minutes, or place it in a microwave-safe container, cover loosely with a white, damp paper towel, microwave on high and check every 30 seconds. To soften hardened white sugar, put it in a sturdy food-quality bag and pound it with a hammer.
evidence.source_title: Check your cooking staples (University of Georgia CAES Field Report)

evidence.claim: WSU Extension: 4–6 months for maximum flavor; microwave 30 seconds
evidence.detail: Brown sugar will keep 4-6 months for maximum flavor. It is extremely important to store brown sugar in an airtight container to retain its moisture and prevent it from becoming hard. Brown sugar can be softened in the microwave covered with a clean, white, wet paper towel for 30 seconds. White sugar will keep at room temperature for 2 years. If white sugar becomes lumpy smashing it into smaller pieces using a meat mallet or hammer can soften it.
evidence.source_title: Cleaning Out the Kitchen Cupboard (Washington State University Extension)

evidence.claim: King Arthur: molasses moisture evaporates; bread overnight; water-and-knead method
evidence.detail: Molasses supplies the moisture that keeps brown sugar soft; when brown sugar is exposed to air for too long, that moisture evaporates. Bread method: a slice of soft sandwich bread sealed with the sugar for 24 hours, or at least overnight, then discard the bread; sliced apple can be used instead. Per Stella Parks: add 3/4 teaspoon (3.5 g) of water per 8 oz of brown sugar to a bag and knead until uniform and soft. Brown Sugar Saver: soak the terracotta disk in water, blot it dry, and place it in the sugar container; it slowly releases moisture back into the sugar, and a reusable Brown Sugar Saver can be added to help maintain moisture. Store in an airtight container or heavy-duty resealable bag with as much air pressed out as possible.
evidence.source_title: How to soften brown sugar (King Arthur Baking, 2026)

evidence.claim: Weight of a packed cup of brown sugar
evidence.detail: Brown sugar (dark or light, packed): 1 cup = 7 1/2 oz = 213 g. Granulated white sugar: 1 cup = 7 oz = 198 g.

original_asset.spec: Troubleshooting table by situation (need it now / need the whole bag soft / can wait a day / dry climate or long storage / white sugar lumps / powdered sugar lumps) mapping to the sourced fix and whether the result lasts. A microwave-method comparison showing why published times differ (amount and covering). A water-dose table scaling King Arthur's 3.5 g per 8 oz: 1 packed cup = 213 g = 7.5 oz → 7.5 ÷ 8 × 3.5 g ≈ 3.3 g (about 0.7 tsp); 1 lb = 16 oz → 2 × 3.5 = 7 g (1 1/2 tsp); 2 lb = 32 oz → 4 × 3.5 = 14 g (3 tsp = 1 tbsp).

cautions: Don't claim moldy, wet, or insect-infested sugar is fine; sources only support that ordinary hardened sugar is usable
Oven-heated sugar is very hot (Domino); don't suggest touching it
Microwave ovens vary; the times are starting points
Shelf-life numbers are quality windows, not safety cutoffs
